docs.title: mini-infer 🚀
docs.text: A minimal, educational, and high-performance continuous-batching LLM inference engine with Paged KV-cache, radix prefix caching, and speculative decoding built from scratch in pure Python and PyTorch.

docs.title: Why mini-infer?
docs.text:
Most practitioners know how to call an inference engine (ollama run or vllm serve). However, the underlying systems engineering that powers modern production LLM serving:

  1. How tensors are paged in GPU VRAM to eliminate external memory fragmentation.
  2. How continuous batching dynamically schedules requests at the token iteration level rather than request level.
  3. How prefix caching avoids redundant prefills across shared system prompts via radix trees.
  4. How speculative decoding accelerates generation by interleaving small draft proposals with target model parallel verification.

...are typically locked behind tens of thousands of lines of complex CUDA, C++, and distributed runtime code.

mini-infer implements these exact production algorithms in pure, readable, testable Python/PyTorch. It runs on consumer hardware (such as an entry-level 6 GB laptop GPU or a free Kaggle T4), with zero C++ compiler or CMake toolchain required.

Our Mission: Safe, Secure, and Optimized for Every Machine

We believe high-performance LLM systems should not require $10,000 enterprise GPUs, cloud API subscriptions, or opaque proprietary silos. mini-infer democratizes modern serving systems, empowering every developer to run autonomous AI agents and personal LLMs 100% privately, securely, and free of cost on everyday hardware.

docs.title: Core Capabilities at a Glance
docs.text: Component Industry Baseline mini-infer Implementation Memory Allocation Static pre-allocated contiguous tensors (60–80% VRAM waste) PagedAttention Block Pool: 16 tokens/block with virtual block tables (< 4% memory waste) Batched Paged Decode (v0.2.1) Serial loop per sequence or custom CUDA kernel Unified [B, 1] Paged Forward Pass: Direct physical tensor gather with zero-overhead slot mapping Prompt Ingestion (v0.2.1) Unbounded monolithic prefill starving decode streams Chunked Prefill: Bounded 512-token chunks interleaving prompt ingestion with active decodes OOM Resilience (v0.2.1) Unhandled CUDA out of memory process crashes Graceful Preemption: Re-queues lowest-priority sequences back to WAITING when pool exhausts Prompt Caching Recomputing \(O(N^2)\) attention on identical system prompts Radix Tree Prefix Cache: Zero recompute on shared conversation prefixes Batching Strategy Naive request batching (waiting for slowest request to finish) Continuous Iteration Batching: Dynamic token-level scheduling Generation Speed Sequential auto-regressive generation (\(1\) token per step) Speculative Decoding: \(K\)-token draft proposals with parallel target verification Model Architecture Black-box weights Pure Qwen2.5 safetensors loader: Custom RMSNorm, RoPE, and SDPA Weight Quantization (v0.2.6) Monolithic FP16 tensors exhausting consumer VRAM Sub-Byte QuantLinear (quantbench-engine): Vectorized INT4 nibble packing (~3.7× compression), INT8 absmax, BitNet ternary, and Ampere 2:4 sparsity

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
• Zero Build Toolchain: No Visual Studio Build Tools, gcc, or nvcc required. Standard PyTorch CUDA wheels power all tensor kernels.
  • Strictly Typed & Verified: Full typing with comprehensive unit tests (pytest) covering KV-cache paging, Radix prefix matching, and speculative verification math.
  • Consumer Hardware Native: Runs comfortably within 6 GB VRAM budgets (RTX 3050, GTX 1660 Ti) while scaling up to cloud GPUs (A10, T4, A100).

docs.title: API & CLI Reference 🛠️
docs.text: mini-infer provides both an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API (built with FastAPI and streaming Server-Sent Events) and an intuitive CLI toolkit.

docs.title: 1. mini-infer info
docs.text:
Inspect hardware environment, PyTorch configuration, and VRAM memory allocation plans.

mini-infer info

docs.title: 2. mini-infer serve
docs.text:
Start an OpenAI-compatible HTTP inference service.

mini-infer serve [OPTIONS]

Options:

Flag Type Default Description --model, -m TEXT Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct Target model name or local path --host, -h TEXT 127.0.0.1 Network interface to bind to --port, -p INT 8000 Port to listen on --num-blocks INT 1024 Number of physical Paged KV blocks --block-size INT 16 Token capacity per physical KV block --device TEXT auto Compute device (cuda, cpu, or auto) --kv-cache-dtype TEXT auto KV-cache precision: auto or int8 (50% memory saving) --quant, -q TEXT None Sub-byte weight quantization: int4, int8, ternary, sparse24 (via quantbench-engine) --group-size INT 64 Block size for blockwise quantization (default: 64)

docs.title: 3. mini-infer repomap
docs.text:
Generate an AST-based repository map skeleton for LLM coding prompts.

mini-infer repomap [PATH] [OPTIONS]

Arguments:

Argument Type Default Description PATH TEXT . Target directory path to recursively index

Options:

Flag Type Default Description --max-tokens, -t INT 1500 Target token budget for AST skeleton --output, -o TEXT None Optional markdown file path to save skeleton

docs.title: 4. mini-infer chat
docs.text:
Interactive terminal coding chat with automatic codebase context and prefix caching.

mini-infer chat [OPTIONS]

Options:

Flag Type Default Description --model, -m TEXT Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct Model name or local checkpoint path --context, -c TEXT None Directory path to index or existing context markdown file --max-tokens INT 256 Maximum generation tokens per reply --device TEXT auto Compute device (cuda, cpu, or auto) --kv-cache-dtype TEXT int8 KV-cache precision: auto or int8 --quant, -q TEXT None Sub-byte weight quantization: int4, int8, ternary, sparse24 (via quantbench-engine) --group-size INT 64 Block size for blockwise quantization (default: 64) --memory / --no-memory BOOL True Enable persistent Agent Memory recall across turns and sessions

docs.title: 5. mini-infer memory
docs.text:
Manage persistent Agent Memory (facts, preferences, decisions, and episodic context).

mini-infer memory [COMMAND] [OPTIONS]

Commands:

  • add: Add a verified cognitive fact. 
    mini-infer memory add "RTX 3050 has 6GB VRAM" --category core --importance 1.5
  • list: View stored memories with decay and access metrics. 
    mini-infer memory list [--category <core|project|decision|episodic>] [--limit 25]
  • search: Query memories using hybrid BM25 + dense subword feature ranking. 
    mini-infer memory search "quantization" [--top-k 5] [--threshold 0.10]
  • stats: Display storage footprint, SQLite path, and category distribution. 
    mini-infer memory stats
  • consolidate: Run cognitive garbage collection, pruning decayed items while preserving core rules. 
    mini-infer memory consolidate [--max-items 500]
  • clear: Purge persistent memories from database. 
    mini-infer memory clear [--category <cat>] [--force]

docs.title: POST /v1/chat/completions
docs.text: Generates an assistant response given a conversational prompt. Compatible with all standard OpenAI SDKs and tools (e.g. LangChain, LlamaIndex, servebench).

docs.title: Request Body (JSON)
docs.text:
{
  "model": "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are an expert AI software architect."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is the primary difference between prefill and decode phases?"}
  ],
  "temperature": 0.7,
  "top_p": 0.95,
  "max_tokens": 256,
  "stream": true
}

docs.title: Streaming Response Format (Server-Sent Events)
docs.text:
When "stream": true, responses are emitted incrementally as standard SSE chunks:

data: {"id":"chatcmpl-102","object":"chat.completion.chunk","created":1740000000,"model":"Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":"The"},"finish_reason":null}]}

data: {"id":"chatcmpl-102","object":"chat.completion.chunk","created":1740000000,"model":"Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":" primary"},"finish_reason":null}]}

data: [DONE]

docs.title: GET /v1/models
docs.text:
Returns list of models currently loaded in memory.

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models

docs.title: GET /health
docs.text:
Returns server readiness, active sequence count, and free KV block pool utilization.

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health

{
  "status": "healthy",
  "active_requests": 3,
  "total_blocks": 2048,
  "free_blocks": 1780,
  "kv_cache_utilization": "13.1%"
}

docs.title: Benchmarks & Systems Evaluation 📊
docs.text: All benchmarks were measured on an entry-level NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 6 GB Laptop GPU (192 GB/s memory bandwidth, CUDA 12.4, PyTorch 2.6.0) to validate high-performance serving under real consumer hardware constraints.

docs.title: 1. KV-Cache Memory Utilization
docs.text:
Comparison between standard contiguous tensor pre-allocation (pre-allocating for 2,048 tokens) versus mini-infer's Paged KV-Cache (16 tokens per physical block):

Workload (Output Sequence Length) Naive Contiguous VRAM mini-infer Paged VRAM Memory Saved Max Concurrency (6 GB VRAM) Short (48 tokens) 1,280 MB / stream 30 MB / stream 97.6% 42 concurrent streams Medium (256 tokens) 1,280 MB / stream 160 MB / stream 87.5% 18 concurrent streams Long (1,024 tokens) 1,280 MB / stream 640 MB / stream 50.0% 6 concurrent streams

[!NOTE] mini-infer achieves \(< 3.8\%\) memory waste across mixed request lengths by eliminating external fragmentation entirely.

docs.title: 2. Radix Prefix Caching Speedup
docs.text:
Measured on identical system prompts of variable lengths (evaluating Time-to-First-Token, TTFT):

System Prompt Length Standard Prefill (TTFT) Radix Cached Prefill (TTFT) Speedup 256 tokens 48.2 ms 6.1 ms 7.9x 512 tokens 98.4 ms 8.4 ms 11.7x 1,024 tokens 210.5 ms 11.2 ms 18.8x 2,048 tokens 465.0 ms 14.8 ms 31.4x

Recomputing quadratic attention on repeated system prompts is completely bypassed; TTFT remains flat at \(< 15 \text{ ms}\) regardless of prompt depth.

docs.title: 3. Speculative Decoding Speedup
docs.text:
Measured using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Target Model) paired with Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Draft Model, \(K=4\) candidate tokens):

Task Type Baseline 1.5B (Tokens/s) Speculative 1.5B + 0.5B Acceptance Rate (\(\alpha\)) Net Speedup Code Generation (Python QuickSort) 19.4 tok/s 42.8 tok/s 84.2% 2.21x Structured JSON Extraction 21.0 tok/s 48.3 tok/s 89.5% 2.30x Conversational Q&A 18.8 tok/s 36.7 tok/s 72.1% 1.95x

Speculative decoding delivers \(\approx 2\text{x}\) throughput improvement while strictly preserving target model mathematically exact output distributions.

docs.title: 4. End-to-End Concurrency Benchmark with servebench (v0.2.1)
docs.text:
Measured live on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 6GB Laptop GPU running Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct via servebench 1.1.0:

servebench run --url http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct --concurrency 1,2,4 --num-requests 12
Concurrency Requests (OK / Fail) Throughput (tok/s) TTFT p50 (ms) TPOT p50 (ms) VRAM Peak (MB) Power Avg (W) Tok/Joule c = 1 12 / 0 13.6 tok/s 556 ms 70 ms 1,544 MB 13.4 W 1.01 c = 2 12 / 0 18.6 tok/s 1,162 ms 98 ms 1,548 MB 13.1 W 1.41 c = 4 12 / 0 27.0 tok/s 2,456 ms 126 ms 1,634 MB 13.2 W 2.04
  • Zero Memory Bottlenecks: Peak VRAM remains capped at 1,634 MB (< 28% of 6 GB laptop VRAM budget).
  • Extreme Power Efficiency: Generates 2.04 Tokens / Joule at \(c=4\) while drawing only 13.2 W of GPU package power.

docs.title: Contributing to mini-infer 🤝
docs.text:
Thank you for your interest in contributing to mini-infer! We welcome contributions from systems engineers, AI researchers, and open-source developers.

Our mission is to build a minimal, transparent, and high-performance continuous-batching LLM inference engine that runs entirely in pure PyTorch on everyday consumer hardware.

docs.title: 🛠️ Development Setup
docs.text:
mini-infer uses Astral's uv for fast, deterministic dependency management.

# 1. Fork and clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/Prajwal7-2002/mini-infer.git
cd mini-infer

# 2. Sync all dependencies into an isolated virtualenv
uv sync

# 3. Verify hardware diagnostics
uv run mini-infer info

docs.title: 🏛️ Core Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
Before submitting a PR, please ensure your contribution adheres to these fundamental design rules:

  1. Pure PyTorch (Zero C++ Compilers):
  2. mini-infer must run on any developer's machine without requiring MSVC Build Tools, CMake, or GCC.
  3. All memory paging, slot mapping, and prefix indexing must remain implementable in standard PyTorch and NumPy.
  4. Deterministic & Testable:
  5. Every new feature must include accompanying unit tests in tests/ that run in under 3 seconds.
  6. Model outputs must match reference implementations within numerical tolerances (\(10^{-4}\) for bfloat16/float32).
  7. Silicon Efficiency:
  8. Keep memory allocations bounded. Dynamic tensor allocations in the inner decode loop (engine.step()) are strictly prohibited to prevent memory fragmentation and GC bubbles.

docs.title: 🧪 Testing & Code Quality
docs.text:
Before submitting your pull request, run the test and lint suites:

# Run unit tests
uv run pytest

# Check code formatting and lint rules
uv run ruff check src tests scripts

# Auto-format
uv run ruff format src tests scripts

# Validate documentation build
uv run mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: 🎯 High-Value Contribution Areas
docs.text:
We actively welcome contributions in the following domains:

  • New Model Architectures: Implementing self-contained, native .safetensors weight loaders for architectures like Llama-3, Gemma-2, or Mistral.
  • Quantization & Cache Compression: Adding native FP8 KV-cache formats or int4 activation scales.
  • Apple Silicon & AMD Support: Validating and tuning performance on Apple MPS and AMD ROCm backends.
  • Optional Accelerated Kernels: Providing drop-in, optional Triton kernels for PagedAttention while maintaining the pure PyTorch fallback path.
  • Scheduler Policies: Implementing dynamic priority scheduling, Fair-Share batching, or deadline-aware chunked prefill.

docs.title: 📬 Pull Request Rules & Submission Process
docs.text: To keep the codebase maintainable and lightning-fast, all contributions must follow these strict rules:

docs.title: 1. Branch Naming Conventions
docs.text: Always create a descriptive branch off main: * feat/short-feature-name (e.g. feat/llama3-loader) * fix/short-bug-description (e.g. fix/radix-hash-collision) * perf/short-perf-description (e.g. perf/fp8-kv-cache) * docs/short-doc-description (e.g. docs/api-guide) * test/short-test-description (e.g. test/chunked-prefill-coverage)

docs.title: 2. Conventional Commit Standards
docs.text:
Format commit messages with clear conventional commit types: 

feat(cache): add dynamic FP8 KV-cache quantization
fix(scheduler): prevent race condition when freeing block 0
perf(engine): optimize slot mapping tensor gather
docs(quickstart): add Cursor IDE configuration guide
test(repomap): add test cases for multi-level inheritance

docs.title: 3. Empirical Silicon Proof Required
docs.text: If your pull request makes any latency, memory, or throughput claims: * You must provide before-and-after numbers measured on real hardware. * State your GPU model, VRAM usage, TTFT, and throughput (tok/s). * PRs claiming "massive speedups" without empirical evidence will not be reviewed.

docs.title: 4. Pull Request Template Checklist
docs.text: When opening a PR on GitHub, our automated PR template will prompt you to verify: - [x] Pure PyTorch Rule maintained (no C++ compilers / CMake required). - [x] Zero dynamic allocations inside the inner decode step (engine.step()). - [x] All unit tests pass (uv run pytest). - [x] Linter and formatter pass (uv run ruff check & uv run ruff format). - [x] Documentation updated and builds strictly (uv run mkdocs build --strict).

docs.title: 5. Instant Rejection Rules (What We Cannot Accept)
docs.text:
• C++ / CUDA Build Dependencies: Any PR that breaks standard pip install on a machine without Microsoft Visual C++ Build Tools or GCC will be closed.
  • Breaking Untested Code: PRs modifying core memory managers without comprehensive unit test coverage in tests/.
  • Megapulls: PRs containing hundreds of lines of unrelated refactors across multiple subsystems. Keep PRs small and atomic.

docs.title: Quickstart ⚡
docs.text: Get an OpenAI-compatible continuous batching engine running on your local GPU in under 60 seconds.

docs.title: From PyPI (Standard)
docs.text: pip install mini-infer

docs.title: With uv (Fastest)
docs.text: uv pip install mini-infer

docs.title: Run Directly with uvx (Zero Install)
docs.text: uvx mini-infer --help

docs.title: From Source (Development with uv)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Prajwal7-2002/mini-infer.git
cd mini-infer
uv sync

[!TIP] Running Commands with uv: When developing from source or within a virtual environment, prefix commands with uv run (e.g. uv run mini-infer info), or activate the virtual environment first (.venv\Scripts\activate on Windows or source .venv/bin/activate on Linux/macOS).

Run the CLI diagnostic tool to verify CUDA availability, detect your GPU, and display the automated VRAM allocation plan and quantization footprint matrix powered by quantbench-engine:

uv run mini-infer info

docs.title: 3. Index Your Project Codebase (mini-infer repomap)
docs.text:
Before querying an LLM about your code, extract an AST skeleton (classes, method signatures, exports) into a compact prompt:

# Generate a ~1000-token repository skeleton
uv run mini-infer repomap ./src --max-tokens 1000 -o repo_context.md

See Coding on Large Codebases for full details.

docs.title: 4. Launching the Serving Engine
docs.text: Start an OpenAI-compatible HTTP inference server. Pass --quant int4 to compress weights by ~3.7× and --kv-cache-dtype int8 to double KV cache capacity:

docs.title: Option A: Sub-Byte INT4 Quantized Serving (Recommended for 6 GB GPUs)
docs.text:
uv run mini-infer serve \
  --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct \
  --quant int4 \
  --group-size 64 \
  --kv-cache-dtype int8 \
  --port 8000

docs.title: Option B: Standard Serving with INT8 KV-Cache
docs.text:
uv run mini-infer serve \
  --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \
  --kv-cache-dtype int8 \
  --port 8000

docs.title: 5. Connect Your IDE or Query via API
docs.text: Once running, send requests via curl or the standard OpenAI Python client.

docs.title: Via curl (Streaming Tokens via SSE)
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
    "messages": [
      {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise AI assistant."},
      {"role": "user", "content": "Explain PagedAttention in two sentences."}
    ],
    "temperature": 0.7,
    "max_tokens": 128,
    "stream": true
  }'

docs.title: Via OpenAI Python SDK
docs.text:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="not-needed")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a fast Python quicksort."}],
    stream=True,
)

for chunk in response:
    content = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
    if content:
        print(content, end="", flush=True)
print()

[!TIP] To connect Cursor, VS Code Continue, or Aider, check the IDE & Client Setup Guide.

docs.title: 6. Running the Unit Tests
docs.text:
mini-infer includes a comprehensive unit test suite covering KV-cache memory managers, dynamic INT8 quantization, and AST repomap logic:

uv run pytest
# Output: 22 passed in 1.87s

docs.title: Persistent Agent Memory Engine 🧠
docs.text: mini-infer includes an embedded, zero-dependency Agent Cognitive Memory Engine (mini_infer.memory). It provides long-term recall, hybrid semantic/lexical retrieval, and automatic prompt context injection across terminal chat sessions—preventing context window bloat and eliminating the need for heavy external vector databases.

docs.title: 1. The Agent Memory Problem
docs.text:
Autonomous AI agents and local inference engines face a fundamental dilemma:

  1. Context Window Limitations: Modern open-weight models (such as Qwen 2.5 0.5B/1.5B) have practical context budgets where KV-cache VRAM grows linearly with prompt length. Cramming entire chat histories and file trees into every prompt causes out-of-memory (OOM) failures on consumer GPUs.
  2. Session Amnesia: Standard terminal chats lose all state once the process exits. User rules, hardware specs, and design decisions must be re-explained in every session.
  3. Heavy Vector DB Bloat: Existing agent memory frameworks (e.g., LangChain, MemGPT, ChromaDB) require multi-gigabyte dependency trees, C++ compilers, external REST servers, or cloud API keys—violating mini-infer's zero-dependency philosophy.

docs.title: The Solution: Embedded Zero-Dependency Cognitive Storage
docs.text:
mini-infer solves this with an integrated SQLite WAL storage layer combined with a deterministic, subword-hashed dense vector embedder and Okapi BM25 lexical ranker running in pure PyTorch/Python standard library.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ mini-infer Interactive Chat / Agent Runner                             │
└───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │ User Query: "What quantization?"
                                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MemoryEngine Orchestrator                                              │
│                                                                        │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │ Hybrid Retriever                                               │   │
│   │                                                                │   │
│   │  Dense Cosine Similarity       Okapi BM25 Lexical Matching     │   │
│   │  (256-dim subword hashing)   + (Term & Inverted Document Freq) │   │
│   │               \                             /                  │   │
│   │                ▼                           ▼                   │   │
│   │           Score Fusion: α · S_dense + (1-α) · S_BM25           │   │
│   │                                 │                              │   │
│   │                                 ▼                              │   │
│   │           Modulate by Importance & Exponential Time Decay      │   │
│   └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                    │                                   │
│                                    ▼                                   │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │ Dynamic Prompt Context Injector                                │   │
│   │ Injects top relevant verified facts into system prompt budget  │   │
│   └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘   │
└────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┘
                                     │ ACID Commit / WAL Fetch
                                     ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Embedded SQLite Store (.mini_infer/memory.db)                          │
│ Indexed on `category`, `last_accessed`, `id` (Zero network overhead)  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 2. Memory Taxonomy
docs.text:
Memories are categorized into a 4-tier cognitive hierarchy:

Category Enum Decay Behavior Description Example Core core None (\(D(t) \equiv 1.0\)) Permanent hardware constraints, developer preferences, safety rules. "RTX 3050 has 6GB VRAM; never exceed 2048 KV blocks" Project project Half-life = 30 days Codebase architecture, module contracts, CLI signatures. "INT4 quantized weights packed in 4-bit uint8 nibbles" Decision decision Half-life = 21 days Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) and trade-off rationale. "Selected BM25+dense hybrid over pure vector for symbol names" Episodic episodic Half-life = 7 days Conversational history, temporary tool outputs, user prompts. "User ran servebench against port 8000 on 2026-10-27"

docs.title: 3.1. Subword-Hashed Dense Embeddings
docs.text:
To avoid downloading a multi-gigabyte BERT or Sentence-Transformers checkpoint, mini-infer computes deterministic 256-dimensional feature embeddings directly in PyTorch:

\[\vec{v}_{\text{raw}} = \sum_{w \in T} \mathbf{e}_{\text{hash}(w) \pmod D} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{w \in T} \sum_{i=0}^{|w|-3} \mathbf{e}_{\text{hash}(w[i:i+3]) \pmod D}\]

where \(D = 256\) is the embedding dimension and \(\mathbf{e}_k\) is a unit one-hot basis vector. The resulting vector is \(L_2\)-normalized:

\[\vec{v} = \frac{\vec{v}_{\text{raw}}}{\|\vec{v}_{\text{raw}}\|_2 + \epsilon}\]

Dense cosine similarity between query \(q\) and document \(d\) is computed via dot product:

\[S_{\text{dense}}(q, d) = \max\left(0, \vec{v}_q \cdot \vec{v}_d\right)\]

This captures morphological similarity (e.g., quantization \(\leftrightarrow\) quant_linear, vram \(\leftrightarrow\) memory) in \(<0.2\text{ ms}\) on CPU.

docs.title: 3.2. Okapi BM25 Lexical Ranking
docs.text:
Dense embeddings can occasionally miss exact variable names or unique file paths. Okapi BM25 guarantees that exact identifier matches receive top priority:

\[\text{IDF}(t) = \ln\left( \frac{N - n(t) + 0.5}{n(t) + 0.5} + 1.0 \right)\] \[S_{\text{BM25}}(q, d) = \sum_{t \in q \cap d} \text{IDF}(t) \cdot \frac{f(t, d) \cdot (k_1 + 1)}{f(t, d) + k_1 \cdot \left(1 - b + b \cdot \frac{|d|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)}\]

where default parameters are \(k_1 = 1.5\) and \(b = 0.75\). BM25 scores are normalized to \([0, 1]\).

docs.title: 3.3. Hybrid Score Fusion & Time Decay
docs.text:
The final retrieval score combines dense semantic score, lexical BM25 score, memory importance weight (\(W_{\text{imp}} \in [0.1, 2.0]\)), and recency decay:

\[S_{\text{final}}(q, d) = \left( \alpha \cdot S_{\text{dense}}(q, d) + (1 - \alpha) \cdot S_{\text{BM25}}(q, d) \right) \times W_{\text{imp}} \times D(t)\]

where default \(\alpha = 0.55\).

docs.title: Exponential Decay with Frequency Reinforcement
docs.text:
For non-CORE categories, time decay follows an exponential half-life curve boosted by total access hits:

\[D(t) = \exp\left( -\frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} \cdot \Delta t_{\text{days}} \right) \times \left(1.0 + \min(0.5, 0.05 \cdot \text{hits})\right)\]

This mimics human long-term potentiation: frequently accessed memories are retained longer even as time elapses.

docs.title: 4. Deduplication & Consolidation
docs.text:
When adding memories via MemoryEngine.add(), incoming content is checked against all existing memories in the category:

  • If cosine similarity \(S_{\text{dense}}(\text{new}, \text{existing}) \ge 0.88\), the engine reinforces the existing memory (incrementing its access hit count and refreshing its timestamp) rather than creating a duplicate entry.
  • MemoryEngine.consolidate() runs cognitive garbage collection, automatically pruning decayed memories when storage exceeds target capacity while permanently protecting CORE items.

docs.title: Continuous Batching & Iteration Scheduling 🔄
docs.text:
Traditional deep learning systems batch requests at the request level (e.g., waiting for all \(N\) requests in a batch to finish generating before returning responses).

Because different requests generate wildly different numbers of tokens (e.g., Request A generates 10 tokens, Request B generates 500 tokens), static request batching leaves GPU cores idle waiting for the longest request:

Static Batching (Request-Level):
Request A: [Prefill][D1][D2][D3][EOS] ──────► [ IDLE / PADDED SLOTS ] ─────► Done
Request B: [Prefill][D1][D2][D3][D4] ... [D500][EOS] ─────────────────────► Done

mini-infer implements Continuous (Iteration-Level) Batching, where the batch is dynamically reassembled after every single token forward pass.

docs.title: Iteration-Level Scheduling
docs.text:
In mini-infer's scheduler (src/mini_infer/engine/scheduler.py):

  1. New Request Ingestion: As soon as a request finishes generating an <|im_end|> token, its KV blocks are freed and returned to the memory pool.
  2. Immediate Slot Re-allocation: A newly arrived pending request is scheduled into the very next forward pass, without waiting for other concurrent requests to complete.
  3. Interleaved Prefill & Decode: The engine multiplexes compute-bound prefill iterations alongside memory-bound decode iterations.
Continuous Batching (Iteration-Level):
Step 1:  [Req A: Token 1]  [Req B: Token 40]  [Req C: Prefill Phase]
Step 2:  [Req A: Token 2]  [Req B: Token 41]  [Req C: Token 1]
Step 3:  [Req A: EOS] ──► Freed!
Step 4:  [Req D: Prefill]  [Req B: Token 42]  [Req C: Token 2]

docs.title: The Prefill vs. Decode Asymmetry
docs.text:
Phase Computational Characteristic GPU Bottleneck Arithmetic Intensity Prefill Processes all prompt tokens in parallel Tensor Compute (FLOPs) High (\(> 100 \text{ FLOPs/byte}\)) Decode Generates \(1\) token sequentially per request Memory Bandwidth (GB/s) Low (\(\approx 1 \text{ FLOP/byte}\))

By co-scheduling requests in decode phase with an active prefill chunk, mini-infer saturates both the GPU's memory bus and its CUDA tensor cores simultaneously, maximizing overall token throughput (Goodput).

docs.title: Starvation Prevention: Chunked Prefill (v0.2.0)
docs.text:
If a single request submits an enormous prompt (e.g., a 10,000-token prompt), naive engines block all existing decode streams for several seconds, causing massive latency spikes (Inter-Token Latency degradation).

mini-infer v0.2.0 solves this with Chunked Prefill: - Chunked Slicing: Prompts are sliced into chunks of chunked_prefill_size=512. - Interleaving: The scheduler ingests at most one 512-token chunk per step, interleaving prompt processing with active decode steps. - Bounded ITL: Time-to-First-Token for the new request proceeds smoothly while active decode streams maintain uninterrupted, steady token emission.

docs.title: Memory Pressure Preemption (v0.2.0)
docs.text:
During burst traffic spikes, requests may demand more physical blocks than available in BlockPool. Without protection, this causes hard CUDA out of memory or MemoryError crashes.

In mini-infer v0.2.0, the continuous scheduler implements graceful Preemption Recovery: 1. When block_pool.can_allocate() fails for active decodes or prefills, the scheduler selects the lowest-priority (most recently scheduled) active sequence. 2. The sequence is suspended and re-queued to the WAITING state, and its physical blocks are freed back to the pool. 3. In-flight high-priority sequences continue uninterrupted to completion. 4. Once blocks are freed by retiring finished sequences, the preempted sequence is re-scheduled and resumed automatically.

docs.title: Paged KV-Cache Memory Management 🧠
docs.text: The Key-Value (KV) cache is the single largest consumer of GPU VRAM in large language model inference. mini-infer implements PagedAttention-style block memory management to eliminate GPU memory fragmentation.

docs.title: The Problem: Memory Fragmentation in Naive Systems
docs.text:
In standard Hugging Face or naive PyTorch implementations, tensors must be stored in contiguous virtual and physical memory addresses.

During autoregressive generation, the output sequence length is unknown ahead of time:

[Request 1: Max 2048 Tokens]  ──► Pre-allocates 2048 slots contiguous VRAM
                                 Actual generation: 42 tokens
                                 Wasted memory: (2048 - 42) / 2048 = 97.9% !

This creates two severe memory bottlenecks:

  1. Internal Fragmentation: Pre-allocating contiguous memory for the theoretical maximum generation length (max_new_tokens) when most requests terminate early via EOS.
  2. External Fragmentation: Dynamic requests of variable lengths allocating and freeing memory randomly, creating holes in GPU VRAM that prevent new requests from batching even when total free memory is ample.

In practice, naive systems waste between 60% and 80% of total GPU memory, limiting concurrency to 2–4 parallel streams.

docs.title: The Solution: Operating System Paging for GPU Tensors
docs.text:
mini-infer borrows the fundamental concept of virtual memory paging from operating systems:

  • Physical Blocks: VRAM is pre-allocated as a single fixed pool of blocks upon engine startup. Each block stores exactly \(B = 16\) tokens for Key and Value projections across all attention layers.
  • Logical Blocks: A client request sees its sequence as a contiguous sequence of logical blocks (\(0, 1, 2, \dots\)).
  • Block Table: A dynamic mapping structure that maps a request's logical blocks to non-contiguous physical block IDs in GPU VRAM.
Request 1 (Logical)           Block Table              GPU Physical Memory Pool
┌─────────────┐             ┌─────────────┐            ┌────────────────────────┐
│ Logical 0   ├────────────►│ Logical 0: 4├───────────►│ Physical Block 4 (VRAM)│
├─────────────┤             ├─────────────┤            ├────────────────────────┤
│ Logical 1   ├────────────►│ Logical 1: 1├───────────►│ Physical Block 1 (VRAM)│
├─────────────┤             ├─────────────┤            ├────────────────────────┤
│ Logical 2   ├────────────►│ Logical 2: 7├───────────►│ Physical Block 7 (VRAM)│
└─────────────┘             └─────────────┘            └────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Memory Waste Analysis
docs.text: With a block size of \(B = 16\) tokens: - Zero External Fragmentation: Because all physical blocks are identically sized (\(16 \times \text{layers} \times \text{heads} \times d_k\)), any free block can serve any request at any layer. - Bounded Internal Fragmentation: Memory waste only exists in the final block of an active sequence: $\(\text{Waste}_{\text{max}} = \frac{B - 1}{N} \le \frac{15}{N}\)$ For a typical request of 400 tokens, average memory waste drops to \(< 3.8\%\), compared to \(> 60\%\) in naive contiguous buffers.

docs.title: Python Implementation: Physical Block Pool & Batched Paging (v0.2.0)
docs.text:
In mini-infer (src/mini_infer/cache/block_pool.py), the physical pool is pre-allocated as a single tensor in GPU VRAM and tracked using a fast stack of free block indices:

class BlockPool:
    def __init__(
        self,
        num_blocks: int,
        block_size: int = 16,
        num_layers: int = 24,
        num_kv_heads: int = 2,
        head_dim: int = 64,
        device: str = "cuda",
    ):
        self.block_size = block_size
        self.free_blocks = list(range(num_blocks))

        # Pre-allocated continuous VRAM tensor: [num_blocks, 2 (K/V), num_layers, num_kv_heads, block_size, head_dim]
        self.pool = torch.zeros(
            (num_blocks, 2, num_layers, num_kv_heads, block_size, head_dim),
            dtype=torch.bfloat16,
            device=device,
        )

    def allocate_block(self) -> int:
        if not self.free_blocks:
            raise MemoryError("Out of KV-Cache Physical Blocks")
        return self.free_blocks.pop()

    def free_block(self, block_id: int):
        self.free_blocks.append(block_id)

docs.title: Zero-Copy Batched Attention Gather
docs.text:
In v0.2.0, gather_batched_paged_kv() gathers past key and value tokens directly from physical memory blocks across all concurrent active decode sequences into a contiguous batch:

# Gathers physical blocks for all active sequences into a unified tensor [B, total_past_len, H, D]
k_all, v_all, mask = block_pool.gather_batched_paged_kv(
    layer_idx=layer_idx,
    block_tables=block_tables,  # List[List[int]] for each sequence
    context_lens=context_lens,  # Sequence lengths
    device=device,
)
This zero-copy gather eliminates redundant DRAM weight transfers and drives continuous batching throughput.

docs.title: Radix Prefix Caching 🌲
docs.text:
In enterprise deployments, conversational agents and coding assistants receive hundreds of requests that share identical system prompts, few-shot examples, or conversation history.

mini-infer implements a Radix Tree Prefix Cache to eliminate redundant prefill attention computation.

docs.title: The Bottleneck: Redundant Prefill Computation
docs.text:
During the prefill phase, an inference engine processes all input prompt tokens in parallel to generate the initial KV cache. The computational complexity of prefill attention scales quadratically with sequence length:

\[\text{Attention Flops} \propto O(N^2 \cdot d)\]

If 100 concurrent users prompt a model with a 1,500-token system prompt, a naive engine executes:

\[100 \times \text{Prefill}(1500) = 150,000 \text{ token FLOPs}\]

With Radix Prefix Caching, the 1,500 tokens are computed once. All subsequent requests reuse the existing physical KV-cache blocks directly from GPU VRAM:

\[\text{Prefill FLOPs} = 1 \times \text{Prefill}(1500) + 100 \times O(1) \text{ Block Table Lookup}\]

Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) for cached system prompts drops from 350 ms down to under 15 ms.

docs.title: How the Radix Tree Works
docs.text:
A Radix Tree (or compact trie) is a space-optimized tree data structure where each edge represents a sequence of tokens:

                              [Root: Empty]
                                    │
                  "You are a helpful assistant..." (Token IDs: [15, 82, 943])
                                    │
                                    ▼
                             [Node A: Block 4]
                             Ref Count: 3
                                 /     \
    "Explain quantum physics..."        "What is the capital of..."
                 │                                  │
                 ▼                                  ▼
         [Node B: Block 7]                  [Node C: Block 12]
         Ref Count: 1                       Ref Count: 1

docs.title: 1. Token Matching & Cache Hit
docs.text: When a new request arrives with tokens \(T\): 1. The engine traverses the Radix Tree from the root, matching token substrings. 2. For every full block of 16 tokens matched in the tree, mini-infer reuses the existing physical block ID. 3. The reference counter of the matching tree node is incremented. 4. Only the unmatched suffix tokens (the unique user query) are dispatched to the model's prefill kernel!

docs.title: 2. Copy-on-Write (CoW)
docs.text: Physical blocks shared across multiple requests are marked read-only. When an active request generates a new token that modifies a partially filled block, a new physical block is allocated and copied using Copy-on-Write semantics, ensuring memory safety across concurrent requests.

docs.title: 3. LRU Node Eviction
docs.text: When the physical memory pool runs out of free blocks, the Radix Tree evicts nodes whose reference count is \(0\) using a Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction policy, returning physical blocks to the free pool.

docs.title: Performance Impact
docs.text: Metric Without Prefix Caching With Radix Prefix Caching Improvement TTFT (1.5k System Prompt) 340 ms 12 ms 28.3x faster Prefill VRAM Allocation 1,500 tokens per stream Shared 1,500 tokens Up to 85% VRAM saved Multi-turn Chat Throughput Degrading with conversation depth Constant low latency 3.2x higher throughput

docs.title: Sub-Byte Weight Quantization & Packaging 📦
docs.text: In mini-infer v0.2.6, model weight representation can be dynamically converted to sub-byte packed integer buffers via direct integration with quantbench-engine.

docs.title: The Decode Memory Bandwidth Bottleneck
docs.text:
During autoregressive token generation (decode phase), batch sizes are small (\(B=1\) to \(B=8\)) and sequence length grows by \(1\) token per step. In this regime, compute intensity is governed by the arithmetic intensity \(I\):

\[ I = \frac{\text{Total Floating Point Operations}}{\text{Total DRAM Bytes Transferred}} = \frac{2 \times P \times B}{P \times \text{bytes\_per\_param} + \text{KV\_cache\_bytes}} \approx \frac{2}{\text{bytes\_per\_param}} \quad (\text{FLOPs/byte for } B=1) \]

On modern consumer GPUs such as the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 6GB Laptop GPU: - Peak FP32 / FP16 Compute: \(9.1\text{ TFLOPs}\) - Peak Memory Bandwidth: \(192\text{ GB/s}\) (128-bit GDDR6) - Ridge Point: \(\frac{9,100\text{ GFLOPs}}{192\text{ GB/s}} = 47.4\text{ FLOPs/byte}\)

Because \(I_{\text{FP16}} = \frac{2}{2} = 1.0\text{ FLOP/byte} \ll 47.4\), single-batch decode runs strictly inside the memory-bandwidth-bound region of the hardware roofline. Compressing weights from 16-bit float down to 4-bit integer cuts DRAM traffic by 73.4%, directly scaling tokens per second on consumer silicon.

docs.title: Supported Quantization Schemes
docs.text:
mini-infer supports 4 drop-in quantization schemes powered by quantbench-engine:

Scheme Target Bitwidth Storage Format Compression Factor Use Case int4 4-bit nibbles Packed uint8 byte buffer + blockwise FP32 scales ~3.7× – 5.0× Maximum VRAM reduction for 1.5B/7B models on 6 GB GPUs int8 8-bit signed torch.int8 + per-channel absmax scales ~2.0× – 2.9× Near-zero perplexity loss serving ternary 1.58-bit 2-bit offset-binary packed buffer + mean absolute \(\gamma\) ~6.0× – 7.5× Extreme compression for BitNet architectures sparse24 2:4 structured 50% condensed float values + 2-bit position metadata ~1.7× – 2.0× Hardware-accelerated Ampere sparse Tensor Cores

docs.title: Vectorized INT4 Nibble Packing (Zero Python Loops)
docs.text:
Storing 4-bit integers in standard PyTorch tensors without packing causes PyTorch to allocate a full 8-bit or 16-bit container per element, yielding zero memory reduction.

quantbench-engine packs two 4-bit signed/unsigned nibbles into each physical uint8 byte purely via vectorized tensor operations:

# Vectorized uint8 nibble packing (pure PyTorch)
low_nibble = q_int4[..., 0::2] & 0x0F
high_nibble = (q_int4[..., 1::2] & 0x0F) << 4
packed_uint8 = low_nibble | high_nibble

During forward execution, QuantLinear unpacks and dequantizes blockwise scales on the fly:

# Vectorized unpacking back to float
low = (packed_uint8 & 0x0F).to(torch.int8)
high = ((packed_uint8 >> 4) & 0x0F).to(torch.int8)
unpacked = torch.stack([low, high], dim=-1).reshape(original_shape)
w_hat = (unpacked.to(torch.float32) - zero_points) * scales

docs.title: Precision Architecture: Preserving lm_head
docs.text:
Quantizing the final vocabulary projection matrix (lm_head, shape [hidden_size, vocab_size] = [1536, 151936] for Qwen2.5) introduces significant perplexity degradation due to extreme logit dynamic ranges.

mini-infer's quantize_model() explicitly excludes lm_head from quantization: - Quantized: q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj across all transformer layers. - Unquantized: embed_tokens and lm_head remain in full FP16/BF16 precision, ensuring sharp output logit distributions.

  --quant int4 \

docs.title: Speculative Decoding ⚡
docs.text: Autoregressive language model generation is notoriously memory-bandwidth bound. mini-infer implements Speculative Decoding to generate multiple tokens per forward pass without altering the target model's output distribution.

docs.title: The Bottleneck: Low Arithmetic Intensity
docs.text:
During the decode phase, generating each individual token requires: 1. Streaming the entire model parameter weight tensor (e.g. 3.0 GB for a 1.5B FP16 model) from GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (VRAM) into fast on-chip SRAM cache. 2. Performing matrix-vector multiplication with a batch size of \(1\).

The arithmetic intensity is approximately:

\[\text{Arithmetic Intensity} \approx \frac{2 \times \text{Parameters}}{\text{Parameter Bytes}} \approx 1.0 \text{ FLOP / Byte}\]

On an RTX 3050 (128-bit memory bus, 192 GB/s bandwidth), loading a 1.5B model takes \(\approx 15.6 \text{ ms}\) per token. The GPU compute cores sit largely idle waiting for weights to arrive over the memory bus.

However, scoring \(K\) candidate tokens simultaneously takes almost the exact same memory-fetch time (\(\approx 16 \text{ ms}\)), because the weight tensor only needs to be read from VRAM once!

docs.title: The Speculative Paradigm: Draft & Target Models
docs.text:
mini-infer pairs a tiny Draft Model with a high-capacity Target Model:

  • Draft Model (\(M_{\text{draft}}\)): Qwen2.5-0.5B (~1.0 GB VRAM, ultra-fast generation).
  • Target Model (\(M_{\text{target}}\)): Qwen2.5-1.5B (~3.0 GB VRAM, superior reasoning and quality).
Step 1: Draft model generates K=4 candidate tokens quickly:
        [x1, x2, x3, x4]

Step 2: Target model evaluates all K candidates in ONE parallel forward pass:
        P_target(x1), P_target(x2), P_target(x3), P_target(x4)

Step 3: Verification (Modified Rejection Sampling):
        x1: Accepted  ✔
        x2: Accepted  ✔
        x3: Rejected  ✖ ──► Sample unbiased token from target residual distribution
        x4: Discarded

Result: 3 tokens produced in the time of a single target forward pass!

docs.title: Mathematical Verification: Exact Distribution Preservation
docs.text:
Speculative decoding is mathematically lossless. The output distribution is guaranteed to be identical to sampling directly from the target model.

For each candidate token \(x_i \sim P_{\text{draft}}\), accept \(x_i\) with probability:

\[\alpha(x_i) = \min\left(1, \frac{P_{\text{target}}(x_i)}{P_{\text{draft}}(x_i)}\right)\]

If token \(x_k\) is rejected, generation halts at \(x_k\), and a replacement token is sampled from the adjusted normalized residual distribution:

\[P_{\text{corrected}}(x) = \frac{\max\left(0, P_{\text{target}}(x) - P_{\text{draft}}(x)\right)}{\sum_{x'} \max\left(0, P_{\text{target}}(x') - P_{\text{draft}}(x')\right)}\]

docs.title: Speedup Analysis & Acceptance Rate
docs.text:
The expected number of accepted tokens per step with draft length \(K\) and average token acceptance rate \(\alpha\) is:

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{Tokens}] = \frac{1 - \alpha^{K+1}}{1 - \alpha}\]

For typical coding and conversational tasks with Qwen2.5-0.5B draft and Qwen2.5-1.5B target: - Average Acceptance Rate (\(\alpha\)): \(70\% - 85\%\) - Draft Length (\(K\)): \(4\) - Net Speedup: \(1.8\text{x} - 2.4\text{x}\) lower latency compared to standard auto-regressive generation.

docs.title: Coding on Large Codebases with mini-infer 🚀
docs.text: How to index, serve, and code on large multi-file repositories using mini-infer on a consumer laptop GPU without running out of memory (OOM) or losing architectural context.

docs.title: The Challenge of Local Codebase LLMs
docs.text:
When developing with local models on consumer hardware (e.g., 4 GB to 8 GB laptop GPUs), developers face three major bottlenecks:

  1. Context Window Saturation: Pasting whole repositories into LLM prompts quickly blows past context limits and floods prompts with implementation noise.
  2. KV-Cache Memory Bloat: In FP16/BF16, storing KV activations for thousands of prompt tokens consumes hundreds of megabytes of scarce VRAM.
  3. Repeated Prefill Latency: Asking multi-turn questions ("explain line 12", "now write tests") forces standard engines to re-prefill the entire codebase from scratch every time, causing 30–60 second latency stalls.

mini-infer solves this with a 3-part systems pipeline: * AST Repo-Map (mini-infer repomap): Compresses entire directories into a dense, typed ~1,000-token skeleton. * Dynamic INT8 KV-Cache (--kv-cache-dtype int8): Drops KV DRAM memory by 48.4% in pure PyTorch. * Radix Prefix Caching: Reuses KV blocks across turns, reducing follow-up Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) by up to 70×.

docs.title: 6. Python SDK Integration
docs.text:
If you are building an automated coding agent, CI reviewer, or custom CLI tool:

from mini_infer import InferenceEngine
from mini_infer.repomap import build_repo_map

# 1. Compress target directory into a 1,000-token skeleton
repo_skeleton = build_repo_map("./my_project/src", max_tokens=1000)

# 2. Boot engine with INT8 KV cache
engine = InferenceEngine(
    "Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct",
    kv_cache_dtype="int8",
)

# 3. Stream coding generation
prompt = f"""You are a senior software engineer. Here is the repository skeleton:
{repo_skeleton}

Task: Implement a new caching layer in `cache.py` matching our architecture.
"""

for token in engine.generate_stream(prompt):
    print(token, end="", flush=True)

docs.title: 7. Real-World Silicon Proof: Synthesizing Code for EdgeSLM
docs.text: To prove zero-hallucination context injection and VRAM stability on physical consumer hardware, mini-infer was benchmarked end-to-end against a production repository (EdgeSLM) containing 15 subdirectories, ONNX quantization engines, and FastAPI endpoints.

docs.text:
• Hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 6GB Laptop GPU (CUDA 12.4, PyTorch SDPA)

docs.title: IDE & Client Integration Guide 💻
docs.text: How to connect mini-infer to Cursor, VS Code Continue, Aider, Cline, and custom OpenAI clients.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
mini-infer implements standard OpenAI-compatible endpoints: * POST /v1/chat/completions (Server-Sent Events streaming) * GET /v1/models

Any tool that works with OpenAI, vLLM, or Ollama works with mini-infer.

docs.title: 1. VS Code (Continue Extension)
docs.text:
1. Install the Continue extension from the VS Code Marketplace.
  2. Open ~/.continue/config.json (or click the gear icon in Continue).
  3. Add mini-infer as a model provider:
{
  "models": [
    {
      "title": "mini-infer Local",
      "provider": "openai",
      "model": "Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct",
      "apiBase": "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1",
      "apiKey": "not-needed"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: 2. Cursor IDE
docs.text:
1. Open Cursor Settings (Ctrl + Shift + J or Cmd + Shift + J).
  2. Navigate to Models.
  3. Under OpenAI API Key, toggle Override OpenAI Base URL:
  4. Base URL: http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1
  5. API Key: dummy (or any string)
  6. Add model name: Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct (or Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct).

docs.title: 3. Aider (Autonomous Terminal Pair Programmer)
docs.text: Aider is an AI pair programmer in your terminal that automatically edits files and creates git commits for you.

docs.title: Launch Aider:
docs.text:
On Windows (PowerShell): 

$env:OPENAI_API_BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1"
$env:OPENAI_API_KEY = "dummy"
aider --model openai/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct

On Linux / macOS (bash/zsh): 

export OPENAI_API_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1
export OPENAI_API_KEY=dummy
aider --model openai/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct

docs.title: 4. Zero-File-Selection Prompting (Direct Instructions)
docs.text:
Developers often ask: "How do I prompt without selecting/pasting files or typing @filename every time?"

Here is how each tool handles zero-file selection:

docs.title: A. In Aider (Autonomous Codebase Navigation)
docs.text:
You do not need to type /add src/api/app.py. Aider automatically reads the repository map: 1. Simply type your goal in natural language: 

> Add a GET /metrics endpoint that returns server uptime and memory stats
2. Aider scans the AST repo map, recognizes that endpoints belong in src/api/app.py, asks Add src/api/app.py to the chat? (Y/n), applies the change directly to disk, and commits it.

docs.title: B. In mini-infer chat -c ./src (Zero Configuration)
docs.text:
Because you passed -c ./src, the entire architectural skeleton is already resident in the model's KV-cache: 1. Type your prompt: 

User: Add a new metrics endpoint returning uptime and GPU memory stats.
2. The model immediately knows where endpoints are defined, crafts the exact code matching your codebase style, and thanks to Radix Prefix Caching, follow-ups respond in < 0.8s!

docs.title: C. In VS Code Continue (@Codebase)
docs.text:
Instead of typing @app.py, use the @Codebase context provider in the Continue sidebar: 

@Codebase Add a /metrics endpoint returning server uptime. Follow existing FastAPI conventions.
Continue will automatically retrieve the relevant files across your entire repository.

docs.title: 5. Python OpenAI Client
docs.text:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1",
    api_key="not-needed",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful software engineer."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Write a Python decorator that retries on exception."},
    ],
    stream=True,
)

for chunk in response:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="", flush=True)
print()
